analysis.one_liner: Lets companies share customers' internet data with the government for cybersecurity, with immunity from lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The House passed CISPA 248-168 on April 26, 2012, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: CISPA would have let internet providers, social media companies, and other private firms monitor their networks and share "cyber threat information" with the federal government and each other, with the shared data routed through a Department of Homeland Security center. It would have given these companies legal immunity for sharing in good faith, exempted what they shared from public records laws, and overridden stricter state privacy rules. In exchange, the government could receive threat data from private networks and could use it not just for cybersecurity but also for certain criminal investigations and national security purposes.
analysis.who_benefits: Intelligence agencies would gain a new legal channel of information flowing in from private networks, plus procedures for sharing classified threat intelligence out to "certified entities" and utilities [S5]. Internet providers, social media platforms, cybersecurity vendors, and other corporations would gain the most: authority to monitor user traffic and pass data to the government, immunity from civil and criminal lawsuits for good-faith sharing, an exemption from Freedom of Information Act disclosure for anything shared with the government, and protection from state privacy statutes [S5]. Ordinary users might see some modest protection from hacking and identity theft through faster threat sharing [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tech companies, cybersecurity vendors, and intelligence agencies

how_it_helps.text: Companies and cybersecurity providers get explicit authority to use monitoring systems to identify and obtain "cyber threat information" and to share it with any entity the protected company designates, including the federal government — a shield against lawsuits claiming such monitoring or sharing violated privacy or wiretapping laws.

The bill grants sweeping legal immunity: no civil or criminal cause of action may be brought against a protected entity, self-protected entity, or cybersecurity provider acting in good faith, for the sharing itself or for decisions made based on the shared information.

Anything shared with the federal government is exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act and under state open-records laws, and is treated as proprietary — so the public cannot find out what was handed over.

The Director of National Intelligence must establish procedures for sharing classified cyber threat intelligence with certified private entities and utilities, and can expedite security clearances for company employees — giving favored firms access to classified government intelligence.

Shared information flows to DHS's National Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Center and can be passed to other federal agencies, giving the government a new stream of data from private networks that may be used not only for cybersecurity but also for investigating cybersecurity crimes, protecting people from serious bodily harm, child exploitation cases, and national security.

analysis.who_pays: Internet and phone users, whose communications and personal data could be monitored by companies and passed to the government without their notice or consent, with no right to sue if it is mishandled [S5]. Anyone relying on transparency is also out of luck: shared information is exempt from FOIA and state disclosure laws, and the bill preempts state statutes that would restrict the authorized sharing [S5]. The general public bears the privacy cost in exchange for whatever security benefit faster threat-sharing actually produces [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Internet users' privacy and legal recourse

drawbacks.text: The definition of "cyber threat information" is broad — it covers any information about threats to a network or data moving through it — and shared information goes to a DHS center and can then be passed to other federal agencies, so personal communications swept up in monitoring could move across the government.

Information shared with the government is exempt from Freedom of Information Act disclosure and from state open-records laws, so the public would have no way to see what companies handed over or how it was used.

Companies get blanket immunity from civil and criminal suits for good-faith sharing, and for decisions made based on the shared data — meaning users would have essentially no legal recourse if their information was shared or used improperly by a company.

The government may use the information beyond cybersecurity — for investigating cybersecurity crimes, protecting people from death or serious bodily harm, child exploitation cases, and national security — and while it may not "affirmatively search" the data for other purposes, the exception list is long.
The bill preempts any state statute that restricts the authorized sharing, wiping out stricter state privacy protections.

The federal government's own liability for violating the rules is capped at actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, with a two-year deadline and the suit as the exclusive remedy — a weak deterrent against misuse by agencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The security case is real but thin: faster sharing of threat data could help companies and utilities defend against hacks [S4], and the amended bill does contain genuine protections — a five-year sunset, exclusions for mere terms-of-service violations, bans on using library, medical, tax, firearm-sale, and education records, an annual Inspector General review, and federal liability for misuse [S5]. But the core trade is lopsided. Companies get immunity, secrecy, and preemption of state privacy laws, while users get no notice, no consent requirement for what companies designate, and no practical way to sue [S5]. The government's permitted uses extend well past defending networks. An honest supporter would concede the privacy cost is concrete while the security benefit is speculative.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide margin, but the Senate committee it was sent to never brought it up, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI) introduced the bill on November 30, 2011; the House Intelligence Committee, which he chaired, considered it the next day and ordered it reported 17-1.

The committee reported an amended version on April 17, 2012 that added restrictions on federal use of the information — no regulatory use, no affirmative searching for other purposes — and replaced the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board review with an Inspector General report.

On April 26, 2012 the House debated the bill under a rule allowing only specified amendments. Rep. Perlmutter's motion to recommit — with instructions to add protections for internet passwords and a ban on a national firewall — failed 183-233, with 182 of 190 Democrats in favor and just 1 Republican.
The bill passed the House later that day, 248-168: 206 of 241 Republicans voted yes along with 42 of 190 Democrats; 140 Democrats and 28 Republicans voted no.
The Senate received the bill on May 7, 2012 and referred it to the Select Committee on Intelligence, where it sat with no further action through the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.

Outside the record, the Obama administration warned in April 2012 that it would recommend a veto because the bill lacked adequate privacy protections, and civil liberties groups and much of the tech community campaigned against it — opposition the Senate never tested with a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary internet users kept the legal protections the bill would have overridden — no blanket corporate immunity, no FOIA exemption for company-government data sharing, and state privacy laws left intact. The Obama administration avoided a veto fight, while the intelligence agencies and companies that would have gained the sharing channel and immunity got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Internet users; agencies and tech firms got nothing

for.name: Mike Rogers (R-MI)
for.role: Chair, House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Wrote and sponsored the bill, steered it through his committee (approved 17-1), set up a rule limiting amendments to a pre-approved list, and managed it to passage on the floor.

for.name: Dutch Ruppersberger (D-MD)
for.role: Ranking Member, House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
for.what_they_did: Co-led the bill with Chairman Rogers and demanded recorded votes to hold the floor coalition together during amendment debates.

for.name: 206 of 241 House Republicans
for.role: House Republicans voting on final passage
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, supplying 206 of the bill's 248 votes.

for.name: 42 of 190 House Democrats
for.role: House Democrats voting on final passage
for.what_they_did: Crossed party lines to vote yes, including the Intelligence Committee's Democratic members.

for.name: Telecom and business lobby
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed the bill, arguing companies needed liability protection to share threat data with the government.

against.name: 140 of 190 House Democrats
against.role: House Democrats voting on final passage
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 140-42 within the party, and backed the failed motion to recommit with privacy instructions (182-1 within the party).

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Warned in April 2012 that the President's advisers would recommend a veto because the bill lacked adequate privacy and civil liberties protections.

against.name: Privacy and civil liberties groups
against.role: Advocacy organizations (EFF, ACLU, internet activist campaigns)
against.what_they_did: Ran public campaigns against the bill, arguing its definitions were too broad, its immunity too sweeping, and its secrecy provisions unacceptable.

against.name: Senate Intelligence Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the House bill after it was referred on May 7, 2012; the chair pursued a competing cybersecurity approach, and the bill never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: 28 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, bucking their party's leadership.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party — 206 of 241 Republicans voted yes versus only 42 of 190 Democrats — and the privacy-focused motion to recommit failed 183-233 along nearly pure party lines, with 182 Democrats and just 1 Republican in favor.

industries.industry: Internet providers and social media platforms
industries.note: The bill gives them authority to monitor user traffic and share data with the government, plus immunity from lawsuits, FOIA exemption for what they hand over, and preemption of state privacy laws. Their legal gain comes directly out of users' privacy and ability to sue.

They gain a broad mandate — monitoring networks and exchanging threat data — plus good-faith immunity, expanding their market and legal cover. Some of their work (stopping breaches) does protect customers, but the immunity removes the main check on over-collection.

industries.industry: Intelligence community and national security agencies
industries.note: The bill creates procedures for the intelligence community to receive information from private networks through DHS's integration center, usable for investigations beyond pure cybersecurity. It does bar affirmative searching for other purposes and codifies an anti-tasking rule, but the net flow of data into government grows.

Electric, gas, telecom, and water utilities are explicitly included and would receive classified threat intelligence via security-cleared personnel, helping them defend against attacks on services the public depends on.
